name: Celeste
lede: Celeste is a very pale, cool cyan whose name means heavenly or sky blue; as a word it is older than the swatch, and the books that mention it use it for sky-blue pigments and cloth.

sections.title: A heavenly name
sections.body:
*Celeste* means heavenly, and in French the same idea is *bleu céleste*, heavenly blue [2]. It belongs to the family of sky words for blue: cerulean comes from the Latin *caelum*, the vault of heaven [2].

The swatch here is a pale, almost icy cyan. Our data does not document where this exact color name entered a system, and the only source in our set is a wiki list [3]. So the swatch should be read as a modern definition of the word, not as a historic pigment.

sections.title: Celeste in medieval Florence
sections.body: The word is old as a name for a blue cloth. In the second half of the thirteenth century, Florentine dyers and buyers saw the red *scarlatto* and *vermiglio* challenged by a run of blue tones, and *celeste* is one of seven named in a note by Pastoureau, beside *persio*, *celestino* and *azzurino* [4]. The note says patrician blue fashions seem to have reached Florence before Milan, Genoa or Venice [4]. Nothing in that list tells us how pale or green any of them was, so the medieval celeste cannot be matched to this swatch.

sections.title: Bleu céleste, the pigment
sections.body:
By the nineteenth century the French phrase was a trade name [1]. Cobalt stannate, a mixture of cobalt and tin oxides, became available as a watercolor in England in the 1860s from the firm Rowney, and by the 1870s as an oil color, sold as cerulean blue in England and *bleu céleste* in France [1]. Ball describes it as having a greenish tinge, a little like azurite [1]. The pigment dictionary files *bleu céleste* as a synonym for cerulean blue and for cobalt tin oxide [5].

Gage's notes point to a 1902 handbook (Vibert) on the reputation of *bleu celeste*, where it is grouped with Prussian blue, among others [6]. Signac was one of the Neo-Impressionists who liked cerulean enough to use it [1][6]. Ball's greenish tinge is not what this icy swatch shows, so treat the swatch as the word's modern color, not the pigment's.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our archive has this color covering at least 1% of its canvas, as photographed [7]. That describes the archive, not painting as a whole, and a pale cyan this bright is rare in aged, varnished pictures [7]. If you want the painted version of heavenly blue, look at [[cerulean-blue]], [[sky-blue]], [[powder-blue]] and [[light-blue]].

origin.first_recorded: as a Florentine blue name by the later 1200s (Pastoureau); this swatch's source origin undocumented
origin.source: Pastoureau, Blue, ch. 12 notes; Ball, Bright Earth, ch. 15

disambiguation.gloss: The pigment sold as bleu céleste is a deeper, slightly greenish blue

choices: Cerulean blue, a cobalt tin pigment

openers: Celeste means heavenly: a thirteenth-century Florentine blue and a nineteenth-century paint name.
In France, cerulean was sold as bleu céleste.

issues: Removed unsupported Italian-etymology claim (Coles gives only Latin caelum and French bleu céleste).
Gage 1902 note reworded to what it says (reputation, grouped with Prussian blue).
Replaced unsourced 'much deeper' cerulean claim with Ball's greenish tinge.
